newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- New Year starts on sour note.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- New Year starts on sour note.

text.p: With New Year's Day festivities behind it, the market will reopen Thursday on an unexpectedly sour note, market participants said.
Champagne bottles will still be uncorked on New Year's Eve, but not with any help from the Treasury market's farewell performance to 1996 hours earlier.

Prices of most U.S. government securities fell sharply on the last day of the year due to a conglomeration of economic reports that, together, painted a rosier picture of the economy than the credit markets had been prepared for.

A jump in new housing starts in November, a December rise in consumer confidence and a firm reading on the manufacturing economy in the Midwest all conspired to alter the U.S. Treasury market's holiday frame of mind.
As a result, as players gradually return to work after the holiday, their mood will be defensive, said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury strategist at UBS Securities Inc.

"I was very constructive on the bond market before Tuesday's data," said Dimick. "I thought the profit-taking that took place in the bond market during December would give players plenty of cash to put to work in the first quarter."
But after the home sales, consumer confidence and Chicago Purchasing Managers reports on Tuesday, participants will be less inclined to increase their market exposure, Dimick said.

"We will bring a defensive attitude into the New Year because (Tuesday's) statistics showed a somewhat stronger economy than people had allowed for," agreed William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"The legacy of these figures will be a cautious trading environment going into the employment numbers," said Sullivan, referring to the December payrolls report due on January 10.
Sullivan said thin trading conditions on Tuesday might have aggravated the market's negative reaction to the data.
But he and Dimick agreed the data would not fade from the market's mindset in the early part of the year.

"There's no reason to buy paper here," said Sullivan. "There is no way the market can rally back to its old highs without evidence that the economy has lost more momentum than these (Tuesday) figures imply."
Dimick said: "Granted these were second-tier numbers. But they are a rather compelling set of information when taken together."
The market does get two fresh pieces of economic data on Thursday -- weekly initial jobless claims and the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) December report.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that jobless claims edged down to 334,000 in the week ended December 28 from 335,000 a week earlier.

"We had a couple of weeks when claims moved up to 350,000, indicating that the labor market was finally cooling off," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Then last week they dropped down to 335,000."
Feinman and other economists said jobless claims data in a week divided by the Christmas Day holiday could be unreliable.
"Any surprises will probably be attributed to faulty seasonal adjustments," said David Sloan, economist at I.D.E.A.
The December NAPM, on the other hand, will certainly be of interest.
"If NAPM is on the weak side, close to 50, the market will respond positively," said Dimick. "But the upside potential is limited after the Tuesday data.
"The bottom line (for the market to go higher) is you need a weak employment report," said Sullivan.
-- North American Treasury Desk ((212-859-1679))
